utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It will be necessary for us to sit without Judge Van den Wyngaert, we believe just this afternoon, and we'll therefore sit in accordance with Rule 15 bis. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just deal with one or two small administrative matters at the start of the week, because it really has to do with the running of the trial. Clearly, there is a continuation of cross-examination today. There will be one more Radic witness to be called, dealing principally with two areas. It may well be that that will not take a long period of time. Then there is, I believe, one final quasi fact witness tomorrow, and I believe Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday we are sitting full days; Friday, the normal day, as I will call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought it was only Tuesday and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I asked certain members and I was told Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. I know we'll all be devastated if we're not sitting a full day on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't get a court on Thursday when I last heard, but if you've found one, Mr. Moore, we're pleased to accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I won't look too hard. In any event, there is an expert to be called on behalf of Mr. Radic. Working out our timings, we had hoped and believed, actually, that that witness would perhaps start his evidence tomorrow, approximately -- well, the afternoon, and we thought that the cross-examination would probably conclude by Wednesday afternoon. Therefore -- well, it may be at the end of Wednesday. But certainly, it brings into play Thursday and Friday, what may occur. We have looked at the case as a whole, and we had hoped that the evidence would conclude in toto by the end of November, perhaps the start of December, and we had believed that it might be possible for the written work, the submissions by both Prosecution and Defence, to be in just before Christmas. Now, that may be an overly optimistic estimate, but certainly it is one of the options that seem to remain. If that isn't the case, then I would have thought, given the holidays, the Christian holidays and the Orthodox Christian holidays in Serbia, it would be unlikely, then, that the written work would not be sought by the Court before the end of the second week in January. And it really, then, begs the question whether, in actual fact, Mr. Sljivancanin will be commencing his evidence on Thursday. The reason I ask is as follows: We have asked twice now for clarification on certain issues, factual issues. The 65 ter summaries are two pages only. We have put in, again, another request for details. But if the case for Sljivancanin were to start on Thursday and it were to go over, what I will call, the four-day break - Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday - that would be analogous to giving the Prosecution notice of the issues that were to arise and therefore we could start on the Thursday or the Friday. I would just seek the Court's guidance in relation to that, because clearly plans have to be made by all parties, both Prosecution, Defence, and obviously the Bench as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I lost the thread partway through. Are you proposing that we move to the Sljivancanin case on Thursday or the following Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest Thursday, because it's two days, it's two full days, and then we would have the equivalent of the notice that is really not obvious in the 65 ter summaries. The 65 ter summaries are still inadequate. They don't deal with factual matters in sufficient detail. We have, again, asked for those details to be clarified. If the Sljivancanin case were to start on Thursday, then he would be through most of his evidence and we would know what the issues would be, and we'd have an appropriate time to consider them. If he were to start on the following Wednesday, without any notice from the Defence or any additional notice, we may find ourselves asking for time because we are not aware, still, of many of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't depend on starting time; that depends upon you receiving additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that will be arrived whether we start on Thursday or the following Wednesday. It should be available at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, one would hope so. But I understand the difficulties my friend has, my learned friend Mr. Lukic has, on time. He has a large case to control. I understand that. What I am concerned about is that proofing notes may come in on Monday or Tuesday of next week, when most people will not be available. That's what's concerning me more than anything else. People have made other arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But isn't that going to happen whether we start on Thursday, if that's possible, or the following Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we start on Thursday, and Sljivancanin gives his evidence - let us say it's two days - then we know exactly what the issues are going to be and we can proceed and continue on the Wednesday, and we make up two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it notice of the evidence -- the factual matters to be dealt with by Mr. Sljivancanin or factual matters to be dealt with by other witnesses that you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Initially, clearly, Mr. Sljivancanin, because he is the trunk of the tree. So it is the Sljivancanin 65 ter summaries that we are concerned about. Clearly, there are other witnesses. It may require amendment by my learned friend Mr. Lukic; it may require clarification. But as matters stand now -- and I don't know if the Court has got the 65 ter summaries. I think it is three pages. And with regard to the 20th, I think it is no more than about six lines. And when one thinks about various issues, for example, did Sljivancanin meet Vujic? Did he speak to Vujic? Did he have the briefing at 6.00 in the morning? How long did Sljivancanin stay at the hospital? Was he part of the re-selection process? Did he ever visit the JNA barracks? Although we have formative of challenge on that. Did he ever visit Ovcara? There are number of matters that specifically relate to the 20th that clearly are matters that concern us and, I suspect, concern the Bench. So we need to have some form of notice, in accurate and precise form, to deal with that. Pulling up transcripts, checking other matters, such as documents, are not always easy; they take time. So if we start on Thursday, then we will have sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you've raised a number of issues. I don't believe all of them can be dealt with today. The first is when you will receive adequate notice of the facts, the material facts, at least, that will be the subject of evidence by Mr. Sljivancanin and then by his other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second is whether the progress of the trial this week will be such that it will be sensible and practical to start the Sljivancanin defence this week, or whether it would be preferably delayed to the Wednesday of the next. Now, beyond that, you're wanting to look into crystal balls about December and January and February or March --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, not February and not March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I keep remembering a year ago, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think at this point it may be too much to ask for, to think that we will have very clear dates about that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let's just deal with the immediate and then see how the future lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not worried for myself. I am not concerned for myself. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, not in the slightest. I live in this jurisdiction and therefore it does not create difficulties for me. But there are other people who have to make arrangements, and they have long ways to travel and it's very difficult to know exactly when it is they are able to book. Those are the people I concern myself for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Even the Presiding Judge might live a little distance from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But Your Honour makes the rules; I only obey them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have to make them within a framework, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, a great deal of interest attaches to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm not sure where to start. I was not thinking about raising that issue today, but Mr. Moore clearly put me to it. As for the length of the Defence case, I thought there was a ruling by the Chamber on that, on how long our case should take; that was certainly my guiding light when I was drawing up my schedule and the specific order of witnesses appearing before the Chamber. As for the summaries, I got an e-mail from Mr. Moore today. We've discussed that already. Although we do normally talk about any problems that might arise, we are working on it and I think tomorrow we'll have a more detailed summary relative to all the points that would be raised in the examination-in-chief. I have no intention of answering Mr. Moore's questions in that summary, but I have every intention of informing him of all the -- giving him notice of all the material facts that the witness will be addressing during the examination-in-chief. This detailed summary will be submitted to both Mr. Moore and the Chamber. Another matter that has arisen and seems to be problematic for me and our Defence team is the following: If, indeed, we start on Thursday - and this is something that I mentioned some days ago; however, there seems to be a rather technical problem now - if we start Mr. Sljivancanin's testimony on Thursday, we only have the next two days left to proof him and be finished by 8.00 in the evening. We saw him today and we have visits scheduled for tomorrow, the day after tomorrow. The authorities from the Detention Unit tell us it normally takes between one and two hours before they can actually talk to us. And 1945 hours in the evening seems to be the latest we can stay there, and yet we have to put him on the witness stand in a condition which can only be described as exhausted, and that applies equally to him and to us. I know you are going to say we have been doing this for a long time, but it's like a college student, you know, we always need one more day. We have been preparing for the 23rd and the 24th of October, to spend these two days proofing the witness for his testimony. This was the principal reason we meant to ask the Chamber to start as previously determined and ruled upon. The deadline is clear, I believe more so than either of the two other Defence teams or the OTP themselves. We know exactly when the trial ends, and that also puts an end to our case. The 33 working days seems to be the framework for our Defence case, and it seems to be set in stone. The evidence, as Mr. Moore has suggested himself, is quite material. We'll make sure to be submitting to him a detailed summary and we'll make sure that he knows anything that he might want to know about any of our future witnesses, any of the documents that we shall be tendering in relation to Mr. Sljivancanin. And we shall certainly abide by the framework set for his testimony. It would be very helpful to us to start his testimony next Wednesday, and Mr. Moore should have sufficient time. At the very latest, the day after tomorrow, he receives a detailed summary and that should allow him plenty of time to prepare properly. What is really not so helpful is we'll spend the following two days in the courtroom, both morning and afternoon, and then putting Mr. Sljivancanin on the stand right after would not be so convenient, whereas we might get the two days next week that we could really use. This is not an application to have the deadline as scheduled extended or deferred. But we think the 25th should be the day we start, first, with a brief opening statement and then with Mr. Sljivancanin's testimony. It is in our best interest to keep track of time and to keep the testimony running according to schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems no inclination of any other Defence team to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has previously indicated that we plan for evidence in the Defence case of Mr. Sljivancanin to finish no later than the Friday, the first full week of December. Mr. Lukic seems at ease in his mind that that can be accomplished with the commencement of Wednesday of next week. To give both Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Lukic and those assisting, on the one hand, and Mr. Moore and those assisting him, on the other, every reasonable opportunity, we will therefore commence the Sljivancanin Defence case on Wednesday of next week. We are comforted by the assurances that there will be attention given in the course of this week and before the end of this week by Mr. Lukic to the concerns of Mr. Moore about notice. That being so, with the long weekend to follow, matters should be entirely on track for a commencement of the evidence on Wednesday of next week. If there are no further reasons to have to delay the trial, that, of course, will lead us to the end of the Defence case by, I think it is, Friday, the 8th of December. We have only the week following, if there is any slip-up or difficulty. I think all parties would see that it would be extremely beneficial for everybody concerned if we can be sure to have the evidence behind us before we break at the end of this year. So, from the Chamber's point of view, we will be proceeding with that objective. I hope it will be with the full and ready assistance of all parties. I think, Mr. Moore, that is as far as we should go today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful. Could I, however, ask for the Court to make an order that we have the supplementary 65 ter summaries by end of business tomorrow. There has been a considerable time for the Defence to prepare these summaries. It is not, I would submit, an unreasonable request, rather than have it open-ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The end of business on Thursday, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, with the utmost respect, is unfair and I would submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may consider that, Mr. Moore, but don't stretch things too far --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- it will be Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- might I indicate why there would be difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have indicated enough. Thank you, Mr. Moore. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Now Mr. Weiner is continue with his questions. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, last Friday when we left off, we were discussing November 19th at the Vukovar Hospital. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you didn't enter the hospital with Captain Radic on November 19th. You didn't walk through the hospital with him, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, with Captain Radic and the soldiers, we came to the hospital and secured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You didn't enter or go inside the hospital with Captain Radic on the 19th, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic was next to the hospital when I found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: At any time did you enter the hospital with Captain Radic? While Captain Radic was inside the hospital, were you with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Captain Radic was not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You never saw him enter the hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Captain Radic was not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it surprise you that Captain Radic testified last week that he was inside the hospital? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Captain Radic in the hospital, nor did I find him there when I reported on the aforementioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what Captain Radic was doing in that hospital, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic was next to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But while he was inside the hospital, you don't know what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found Captain Radic next to the hospital. I don't know whether he had been inside, because he was next to the building, on the external side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were outside the building, searching for clothes and other objects, you don't know what Captain Radic was doing, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we were not searching for these clothes; we just found them. As far as I know, as far as I know, Captain Radic was outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But if you were on the other side or in the back of the hospital, you couldn't tell where Captain Radic was; that's why you had to go look for him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when I found Captain Radic, he was outside the hospital, on the external side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ask him whether or not he went into the hospital when you found him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat the question, because I did not hear it right through these headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure, sir. When you found Captain Radic, did you ask him if he went inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. When you found Captain Radic, did you ask him if he had gone inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you had asked him. And what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat your question because I was being interrupted twice. I didn't manage to hear your question. I mean I didn't hear the interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly. When you found Captain Radic, did you ask him if he had gone into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ran up to Captain Radic and I reported to him about what I had found. Captain Radic, in that area where he was, ordered the soldiers to be in a state of full combat readiness. And together with him, I ran in the direction which I marked on the sketch and we ran to that place. So I did not talk to Captain Radic; I just reported to him what it was that we had found.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now -- so that's no. So when you saw Captain Radic, you said you warned him that there could be an ambush, that it was a dangerous situation. Sir, in the anticipated testimony -- I'm sorry, in the summary of anticipated testimony, the two of them filed in July of 2006, that statement that you warned Captain Radic of some danger was never included. Isn't it true that you're stating that -- that you stated that for the first time on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, but that statement that you referred to, whose statement is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is a statement of the Defence -- two statements of the Defence that they filed as to your anticipated testimony, and there is nothing in either statement filed in July of 2006 in relation to your testimony today and Friday, relating to you warning Captain Radic. Are you just stating this for the first time on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in that period of time, when I said that I had given a statement, I had not given any statement to anyone. The first statement that could have come from me could have come only from 1500 hours on the 13th of September, from the moment when I got the paper that was a waiver from keeping state secrets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like the terminology used to be more precise, because the interpretation that the witness received was that he made a statement to the Defence and that is probably why there is this confusion on the witness's part. We also seem to have a problem with the microphone. Could my colleague put it in terms of proofing notes, not statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether that helps, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, that foreshadows the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your most recent proofing notes, the notes that the Defence filed with the Prosecution on October 12th, last Thursday, there is nothing in that statement in relation to your warning Captain Radic about a potential ambush. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival here, I talked to the Defence but it was about what and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So does it surprise you, sir, that there is no statement -- I'm sorry, no reference in the proofing notes in relation to your warning Captain Radic? Did you ever tell anyone prior to testifying Friday and today that you, in fact, warned Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on Friday and now I've repeated it. I warned Captain Radic of this danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then you testified, sir, that Captain Radic said something along the lines of -- no, actually, Captain Radic ran after you. Is that correct? That's what you testified to at page, I believe, 13.006; that he ran after you and caught up to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the report, I set out and Captain Radic set out. Now, who was in the front and who was in the back, at this point in time, I cannot say. But that's the way it was. We set out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on Friday that he ran after you. Did he run after you or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you indicated that Captain Radic called the officers and told them: "Maximum combat alert. Prepare for action." You said that twice on pages 1306 -- I'm sorry, 1307 -- I'm sorry, 13.007 and 13.008. Did that happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to Captain Radic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Did Captain Radic then yell: "Maximum combat alert. Prepare for action"? That's the question before you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, in the proofing notes that were supplied by your -- by the Defence counsel as to what you were going to testify to on 12 October 2006, there is nothing about that happening. Did you just make this up, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I experienced, what I saw, what I carried out, I said all of that. Now, whether the Defence omitted to ask me about this or not, I don't know. I told you what happened, and that is what I'm here for, to tell the truth about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it surprise you that Captain Radic testified last week and he never testified as to such an incident occurring? Does that surprise you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I did at that given point in time. I saw; I reported. We took measures related to combat readiness. And I drew this for you exactly. I drew this for you exactly; the place, or rather, the direction in which Captain Radic moved together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So does it surprise you that Captain Radic never testified to any such incident occurring? Does it surprise you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to testify about my knowledge and what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Major Tesic gave a statement and he never mentions this situation occurring. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I say that I said to you and presented before this honourable Court what happened and how things were. What others stated, I don't know. I know what I experienced, what I saw, and what I carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Captain Bojkovski has given a statement. He never testified -- he never gave a statement indicating that this happened. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying that I don't want to make any comments regarding what others stated. I am talking about what I experienced, what I saw, and what I carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we know, sir, that there was never an ambush and no such situation ever did, in fact, occur. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found uniforms that were packed in the container. And if we found weapons, the first assumption as to what this was could only be that somebody threw that away, is hiding somewhere, camouflaged. And we did not know what kind of weapons they had, and whether they had any at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Do you agree that no such ambush ever occurred? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what we saw, first and foremost, we professionals can - how should I put this? - can have a suspicion that there is an ambush, because these uniforms were thrown away and there were discarded weapons, too. Now, whether there was an ambush or not, I cannot say. We could not check that. We could not wait for a possible attack, in case of which we would sustain losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you know, sir, there was no such ambush or attack that day. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no attack, but I would like to point out that on the basis of the discarded uniforms and weapons, the assumption was that there were more weapons somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, the question was: Was there an attack? There was no attack. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no attack, and it is fortunate that there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you, sir, that there was never -- that this incident never occurred, that you made this up. And you made it up to remove Captain Radic from the hospital, because he admitted last week in his testimony that he was inside that hospital. Isn't it true that you made this incident up, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when we arrived to the hospital, when we -- from the moment when we arrived to secure the hospital and up to the moment when we left that area, when we handed over to the other units in charge, things were exactly the way I drew them for you. As a matter of fact, on that day, I said to you, when I drew this position, that you should not think because -- this had to do with a tree; at that time the tree wasn't that way. You shouldn't think that any of our soldiers were on the tree, but rather, underneath. I drew you exactly the position of the container. You have concrete data on that sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 14 today you mentioned "waiver," and you mentioned that on Friday at page 13.054. You started mentioning speaking to the Defence and you mentioned "waiver." During your testimony, on page 13.054, you took a piece of paper from your pocket and you said that you received a waiver on September 13th; and today you said -- at September 13th, did you say at 3.00 p.m.? Did you say at 1500 hours was when you received your waiver? That's on page 14. 1500 hours, 3.00 p.m. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of September, at 1450 hours, at the ministry, or rather, at the Centre for Cooperation with the Hague Tribunal, I signed a document, a waiver, allowing me to disclose state secrets. Practically from that moment the Defence could communicate with me. They were here, though, so they were not in a position to communicate with me. But this document does not pertain to those other points about which you wanted to talk to me, and those were the points upon which your colleagues pressured me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, you received the waiver at approximately 3.00 p.m., or 1500 hours, on September 13th. Now, you went to an interview in Belgrade with the Office of the Prosecutor on September 15th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you met with an investigator and a prosecutor from the Office of the Prosecutor. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were two representatives and a lady who was interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were there, sir, for just under an hour. Let's say approximately one hour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us, how long were you there, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 1355 when I entered the building. At 1400 hours sharp, the interview started. It took about an hour. I left the premises at 1540 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were there, you stated repeatedly that no waiver had been received. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at least five times during an interview, you explained that you were waiting -- awaiting the waiver document from the government. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. It wasn't just five times; it was many more than that. I told them that I was waiting for a waiver to be served on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You told them that many times, even though you've testified in this courtroom, two days earlier, at 2.55 p.m., you had received that document of waiver. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received on the 13th of September and that I signed is a document sent by the Defence, and it states in no uncertain terms there is this request by the Defence for a waiver; therefore, this was a waiver for the Defence's purposes solely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know that that document does not say it was a waiver for Defence purposes. You were shown a government document by the Office of the Prosecutor, saying a waiver had been issued. And when asked about whether you received a waiver on behalf of the Defence, you denied that, too, sir, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's one thing I'd like to ask you. You're talking about information. Can you please ask me one step at a time, in a manner of speaking, so that I might be able to provide specific answers. And I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never stated that you had a waiver, that you had received a waiver on the 13th; in fact, you denied it. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I denied that in front of your representatives because -- the document is crystal clear about that. I'm sorry I don't have it on me right now, but it says, "A waiver is hereby granted pursuant to a request from attorney-at-law Borovic's office." The document that you wanted was something that I received on the 21st. The Government of Serbia signed it on the 21st, and I think it was on the 26th, or possibly the 29th, that I physically received that same document in relation to you. I'm talking about those eight questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you denied ever receiving a waiver - isn't that correct? - even though you had, in fact, received one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received was in relation to the Defence and not the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't even tell them that you received a waiver. Isn't that correct? You denied receiving a waiver from anyone. That wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received from the Defence is a confidential one. It was for the Defence, not for the OTP; these are two crucial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, they showed you a government document saying that the waiver had been issued. You knew that it had been issued on behalf of all parties, sir, and you denied. They asked you specifically and you denied. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No to both of the things you've just suggested. What I denied is what I said. That was the previous document. The document that your colleagues were showing me could have been written by anyone. That's what I'm telling you. And I apologise, please try not to interrupt me. Because the document had no stamp on it, no signature -- I apologise, please don't interrupt me. I would like to be given a chance to finish my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please answer the questions you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a transcript here of that interview. May I pass them out to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We also have the oral statement. We can play the statement and have it translated. The others are for the interpreters. If you could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you if you recall this portion of your statement. It's on page 3; it's the sixth paragraph down or a third up from the bottom. It's in English, but we can play it also for you in Serbian. "Q. To inform you that the Court in The Hague, the Tribunal in The Hague, has been informed by Mr. Radic's lawyers that waivers for you and others were issued on 7th -- on the 7th of September. Have you been contacted, either by telephone or personally, informing you that a waiver has been issued for you?" And your answer is: "A. No. "Q. Does that mean that you have never seen a waiver or have been contacted about a waiver?" Page 4: "A. In only have information" - that should be "I" - "I only have information that the procedure has started." Do you recall those statements, sir, those questions and your answers?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on. What is your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that that document was based on Mr. Borovic, the attorney-at-law, and that I had received a waiver for Defence purposes, I said that this -- that I did not get a document for you. And that's what I thought. It's not business-like to give someone one document so that the other person can misuse it, because your questions have nothing to do with the one question that I received pursuant to Mr. Borovic's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, the question was that you were asked: "To inform you that the Court in The Hague, the Tribunal in The Hague, has been informed by Mr. Radic's lawyers that waivers for you and others were issued on the 7th of December" - I'm sorry - "September. "Have you been contacted, either by telephone or personally, informing you that a waiver has been issued for you?" And you answered: "No." First, do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document signed by the Government of Serbia is dated the 9th of September. I don't know what happened before then. I'm not interested in any agreements, and in particular that goes for that document of yours which bore neither a stamp nor a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is: Do you remember saying "No," in answering that question? Or I would be happy to play that portion of the interview for you. Would you like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For your purposes, I did not have a waiver on me. It would have been unprofessional for me to say back then -- unprofessional, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you did, in fact, say no. You said no in answering that question. Isn't that correct? When you were asked about a waiver, you said no. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were numbers being mentioned about authorisation of some sort. I said: "No, I don't have that document. I have never seen it and I don't know that it exists." This is a document for the purposes of the Defence, not the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, they've asked you, based on a statement from Mr. Radic's lawyers, had you been contacted by telephone or personally informing you that a waiver has been issued for you? And you said no. Isn't that correct? Yes or no, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody had informed me on the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, I'm sorry, I wanted that passage to be concluded before turning to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't going to raise an objection about the substance of this question. I just wanted to see what sort of a document it was that was given to the witness, because what we have received now is a transcript of the witness's interview which took place in Belgrade. It's in English. I know for a fact the witness doesn't understand English, and I thought that he might perhaps use a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document, we're told, is a transcript of the conversation that was in the witness's language being interpreted to it and his answers, of course, being in that language. Carry on, please, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move to another part of that interview; page 7, just after "33 minutes." Do you recall this part of the interview, sir: "Q. Have the lawyers of Mr. Radic ever contacted you to say that a waiver has been issued? Just yes or no. "A. No. "Q. Thank you. All right. Can I take it, then, that if you had a waiver served personally on you, you would have been willing to have an interview with me? "A. Well, that would be my duty. It's no question whether I'm -- I will be willing. Since I received the summons, I have to respond to the summons." Do you recall that passage during the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that I had responded to the summons. When I realised that I had a piece of paper being foisted on me in a bid to convince me that this was a waiver, with no signature, no stamp, no nothing, just a piece of paper which your colleagues were trying to convince me was a valid waiver, I had to refuse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you had already received notice two days earlier of a waiver that allowed you to provide information in relation to military actions, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received several days previously, mind you, was in relation to attorney-at-law Borovic's request, whereas the waiver that I received for your purposes was received for the 26th or the 29th of September. I can't quite remember. Be that as it may, as of that date, you would have been able to get in touch with me and to do the interview, which is not something that you actually ended up doing. There are documents in the archives of Serbia's government to show that. You can verify that for yourself. There is such a document in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never said on September 15th, at the offices in Belgrade, that you had received a waiver on the 13th. First, isn't that correct; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed then, and I still believe, that I was under no obligation to inform you, because this document was not issued at your request and it is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never stated at those offices in Belgrade that you received a waiver at the request of the Defence, did you, sir? You never said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I share anything like that with you? Would that be a business-like thing to do? It's a Defence document. Why should I be mentioning that to you? I am a Defence witness, after all, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's obvious, sir. Sir, you never said at that meeting that "I've received a document of waiver and that I'm awaiting a second waiver from the government." You never said that either, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received was in relation to Mr. Borovic's request. We were expecting yet another document from Serbia's government, at your own prompting, which was eventually received on the 26th or the 29th; I can't quite remember. But it had been signed on the 21st of September by Serbia's government, for your own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the first waiver you received wasn't a Defence waiver; it was a waiver allowing you to speak. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With you, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you falsely maintained that you had no waiver on September 15th, when, in truth, you had received that waiver at 2.55 on September 13th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I got was for the purposes of the Defence. It is a business secret. In our country, in Serbia, that is what it is called. As for a document that you sent to me, I cannot show it to the Defence. If it was a document at the request of Mr. Borovic, then it is a document at the request of Mr. Borovic, and then I would have talked to him. However, at that time they were not in a position to do so. You could not abuse that document and conduct an interview with me, because the questions that you mentioned, those eight, do not coincide with the questions that are based on Mr. Borovic's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been in the military long enough that you know the rules, and when a waiver is issued, you're allowed to speak. It's not for one party; it's not for the other. Isn't it true that you lied when you said that no waiver had been issued, when you, in fact, had a waiver in hand? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note and I repeat: The document that I received had to do with the following, and it says quite literally: At the request of the Borovic law office. And that is how I got the waiver so that I could speak. The second document that I got says, literally, questions for which I got a waiver for the purposes of the international Office of the Prosecutor, and that is appreciated and that is taken into account. If it's for Mr. Borovic, then it's only for Mr. Borovic; if it's for you, then it's only for you, and it can be no other way. After all, that's what the document itself says. Unfortunately, I haven't brought it along, this document, but by way of fax, the Government of Serbia can submit it to you and you can see what it says, quite literally: At the request of Mr. Borovic and the Defence team. And the second document: For the needs of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you had waiver, you had the ability or the right to speak, and you didn't and you lied about it on September 15th. Isn't that correct? Because you never said you had a waiver on that date. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that the document I received is for Mr. Borovic, attorney-at-law. It would be unbusiness-like and unprofessional to give that document to you so that you would abuse it. That is why I said: No, I did not receive it. For your purposes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you lied; you said something that wasn't true. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for whether I lied or not, it is something that the honourable Court is going to decide on. If they wish to see these documents, they will see these documents where it says, literally: For the purposes of the Defence and for the purposes of the Office of the Prosecutor. So you could not abuse that document that was for Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to one last area, sir. Are you aware, in late October 1991, that an assault group was formed - Are you aware of that? - along the axis that Captain Radic had or possessed? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assault group? I don't know about that. I know that there was an assault detachment. As for an assault group, I don't know. And that was at the beginning of October, not at the end of October. That's when the assault detachment was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that within an assault detachment -- Major Tesic's assault detachment, there were three assault groups, of which Captain Radic oversaw one of them? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was an assault detachment, and I know that there was our company, the 3rd Company. As for other names of companies, I'm not aware of any. I know there was the 3rd Company, the 2nd Company, and the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that Captain Radic would control and plan combat activity for the 3rd Assault Group? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Company, yes, JNA units; as for the rest, I don't know, especially assault group. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Captain Radic would draw up plans for actions and issue tasks based on these plans to the assault group commanders? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for three questions put by my learned friend Mr. Weiner on the existence of an assault group, the witness said that he did not know of the existence of an assault group on three occasions. So I believe that this line of questioning is no longer appropriate and should not be pursued any further. He said that he had heard of an assault detachment but that he had not heard of an assault group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner is, I think, putting his case, which is to the contrary, over these matters. That's appropriate. Carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Captain Radic would draw up plans for actions and issue tasks to the assault group commanders based on those plans? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a few moments ago and I'm saying it once again: I don't know about assault groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Captain Radic would receive orders from the brigade and battalion and pass those orders along to the assault -- actually, issue those orders to the assault group commanders? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the word "order" that you used. Are you referring to actual orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, actual orders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic got orders, specific orders, from the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Captain Radic would receive those orders and he would pass them along to the assault group commanders, which included Miroljub Vujovic and Kameni Lancuzanin -- Kameni Lancuzanin? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic received orders every day, every evening, from the battalion command, and he only issued orders to us, carrying out the orders that he had received. He commanded the 3rd Company. I'm not aware of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, that Captain Radic was solely responsible for planning combat operations of that assault group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic received orders from the commander of the battalion, who studied and planned actions for the 3rd Company of the JNA. Captain Radic, that is to say, did not issue orders on his own, as you had put it; he received orders, studied them, and made decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Did Captain Radic draw up plans for combat actions and then issue those tasks to the assault group commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic, upon returning from the battalion command where he had received assignments, would study for the following day, how the day after that would develop. As for assault groups, I don't know about that. We didn't have that. I told you about assault detachments. We had that. But assault groups, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you familiar with the 82-millimetre Mortar Platoon of the TO, the 82-millimetre Mortar Platoon of the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're talking about the mortar platoon that was commanded and guided by Lieutenant Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said on Friday, Lieutenant Hadzic led that unit of the JNA, not of the Territorial Defence, as you had put it just now, especially that company, whatever. I don't know about that. He commanded active troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that Captain Radic tasked Lieutenant Hadzic to command, to observe, and to guide the firing during combat actions of that TO mortar platoon or mortar company? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Captain Radic gave orders and planned the activity of mortar fire, or rather, the firing preparations 10 or 15 minutes perhaps before an operation, I know about that. But that Lieutenant Hadzic commanded and had the TO under him, as you had put it, that is not true. Lieutenant Hadzic did not have the TO within his composition. He had only active-duty soldiers and reservists. These are units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's interesting that you say it's not true, because that's the testimony of Captain Radic, at page 12.622, and I quote: "I didn't trust anyone else sufficiently, apart from him, to guide mortar fire by way of support for the assault group attacking. Therefore, that task of commanding, observing and guiding mortar fire - and the mortars we used were 82-millimetre calibre - I gave that task to him. He was not the commander of that platoon of the 82-millimetre mortars but, rather, during combat he commanded that platoon since I knew that the soldiers from the TO were trained to use mortars, but I didn't know exactly to what extent they could command and guide mortar fire. And for purely security and safety reasons, I appointed him to command." Those are lines 1 through 10 of page 12.622. Are you saying that Captain Radic did not testify truthfully when he said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I know Captain Radic, I know his mode of command, what you read out to me just now looks like a statement of your own. Captain Radic could not have issued this kind of order because he is a trained officer of the then-JNA. What you told me about just now is something that makes no sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it would make sense if that TO unit was subordinated to Captain Radic; therefore, he could assign one of his subordinates to command it and to supervise it. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO units, no; the active-duty soldiers, yes. But not command, as you say, but to guide fire and carry out orders that he had received from Captain Radic. According to what you read out to me just now, it seems that Lieutenant Hadzic had the freedom to take action whenever he wished to do so, without any plan. No. Action was carried out, along with proper control and with active-duty soldiers, without members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it time for the break? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that Captain Radic would plan each evening, for the next day's military activity, the next day's military actions, for a group along his axis, which included the Leva Supoderica unit and Miroljub Vujovic's portion of the Vukovar TO. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic, upon receiving his assignments, or rather, orders from the battalion command, would come to the observation post in that company office, the one that you called a meeting room; but at this company office, he would study his assignment and assess the following day in terms of how this activity would evolve exclusively for the JNA units. Captain Radic did not plan actions; he only studied tasks that he had received from the superior command, that is to say, the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Radic plan combat operations; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic, when receiving a task, would study it and pass a decision for the following day; that is to say, that Captain Radic did not plan. He would only receive tasks, study them, and then pass decisions for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to read a portion of Captain Radic's testimony where he said he did do so. Page 12.620, lines 14 through 20; 12.620, lines 14 through 20. "A. If one wants to control and plan any combat activity, be it an attack or a defence, excuse me, one needs to do that thoroughly because the outcome of that operation depends on it. Since I mentioned a moment ago that I was the only officer who had completed the military academy, I didn't want to leave it to chance that anyone should plan combat operations except for myself. This means that Miroljub Vujovic didn't know how to do that. I also knew that Milan Lancuzanin couldn't do that." Sir, isn't it true that it was Captain Radic that was planning the combat activity for those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic, upon receiving tasks from the battalion commander, studied these tasks, and it is not correct that in our company he was the only one who had completed the military academy, as far as I managed to understand this. There was also Lieutenant Hadzic who had completed a four-year military academy. And it was only the 3rd Company of the JNA that he commanded; that is to say, these tasks that he received, he studied and then passed decisions for the following day; that is to say that Captain Radic did not plan combat activity on his own. He would study the tasks received and make decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Captain Radic testified on page 12.621: "... I always issued those orders to those commanders which were part of the assault group immediately prior to going into action, that is the morning. If we were to start attacking at 7.00 a.m. and if we were all assembled at 6.30, I used to issue those tasks 10 to 15 minutes before we were supposed to set out." Wasn't Captain Radic issuing tasks to other units other than the 3rd Company -- 3rd Motorised Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic did issue tasks in the morning. You gave a particular hour. Let it be the way you put it. Maybe it was 8.00 or 9.00. It all depended on the weather conditions and whether there was any action on that day or not. But it was only in relation to the JNA units, not these so-called assault groups. I don't know about these assault groups. I do not know about him issuing anything to these assault groups. And he did not issue tasks to anyone else but the 3rd Company of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, isn't it true that Captain Radic established the system of communication in that he was the person who set all the codes for each military action? So he knew, by codes, what the name was for each group or squad; he knew what the code was for each geographical terms -- I'm sorry, each geographical location; and that he was the only person who knew all of these codes. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What codes are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The codes before going into combat. So if he wanted to talk to someone on the Motorola, they'd identify themselves in code; they'd say where they were in code. And we're talking about all units along his axis. He was the only one who knew the codes because he was the one who drew them up. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Captain Radic was not the one who drew up the codes. In our company, there were two radio communications devices, and the codes were issued by the battalion command. Now, was it for a day or two or three, whatever, they would change the codes so that the enemy could not intercept our frequencies. But it was the battalion command that did that, not Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to read Captain Radic's testimony on page 12.620 into 12.621; on 12.620, lines 21 to 25, and the first three lines of 621: "In order to protect the data and the system of communication, I did that exclusively. This means that each evening, after daily activities had been completed, I withdrew to a separate room and I drew up the communications systems for each squad leader separately, using code names which usually included various colours, geographical terms and so on and so forth. This was done so that, in the process of communication, no one but me could know who I was talking to and where the particular unit or part of the unit or squad is at that moment." Do you agree with that testimony, sir, of Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our company there were two radio devices. There was Captain Radic and Captain Hadzic. For the codes, you should ask the Supreme Command. Changes were made by him, perhaps, if the superior command told him to do so. As I said on Friday, a company commander is a person who carries out orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, since you're not aware of the assault group in the area, I'm going to ask no further questions at this time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'll ask you several questions in re-examination. The questions will be about your evidence so far as a whole, both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On Friday you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Weiner about rules called the company and platoon rules, and he showed a copy of this to you on the monitor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that being shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is, I suppose, no need for me to show you the rules again. I'll just ask you a question about them. Back in 1991, during your time in Vukovar, can you tell us, what was your so-called military specialty or VES?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was from the quartermaster's unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Back in 1991, were you familiar with the infantry rules? Were you supposed to study those and know them well, back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, these should be studied just because of the relative competencies so that we, too, are in the loop.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't a binding thing, was it, nor did you ever take any exams on those rules in relation to platoons and companies, the rules that we discussed and that was shown on your monitor on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no obligation, nor were we made to take any exams on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. You said as much. Just in order to avoid going back to private session, let us just not mention it altogether. I do, however, wish to dwell on the same subject. So, sir, given how you described your own duty and given the fact that you were a quartermaster in terms of your military specialty, can you please tell us if you were part of the control and command system at the time. I'm talking about the autumn of 1991, the month of November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not part of the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now be moving on to something else, something that my learned friend Mr. Weiner has exploited to quite a high degree. It's about you arriving at the hospital, when you set up an external security system there. Mr. Weiner told you what the battalion commander, Borivoje Tesic, said about those events. Now, sir, in relation to the time when you were securing the hospital - and you told us on Friday that the battalion commander did eventually come to the hospital - can you tell us whether the battalion commander, or rather, when he came, and would he have been able to see or hear you report to Captain Radic about what you had come across in the hospital yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Commander Borivoje Tesic arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Last Friday you were asked by the OTP - for my learned friends' benefit, the reference is page 56 - and I quote, you said: "The company commander's meetings were held at the command post of the 1st Battalion." Can you tell us when the commander of your company, Miroslav Radic, went to those, as you called them at the time, meetings, or rather, those briefings? When, what time of day, and how long would these meetings normally take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Radic would go to the command every day. He would do this every day, in the evening. I can't be more specific about the time, but it was certainly after 1900 hours. He would stay between an hour, an hour and a half, depending on the situation. But it was always in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you about what went on in Belgrade. My colleague asked you all sorts of questions about this. You said the first request was submitted by the Borovic law office for a waiver to be granted you. So, sir, what exactly were you thinking when you were told that there had been -- that there had been a request put in by the Borovic law office? Who, at that point in time, would have been authorised to ask you questions about the subject matter that the waiver was in relation to or that the waiver was covering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received two documents. The first document was dated the 13th of September. It was the Defence, and the Defence alone, that would have been authorised to ask me questions about that. As I've told the Prosecution, there was something else that I had not yet received, because previously I had been mentally harassed and humiliated about this purported waiver. I wanted to keep them from misusing that document, and that was why I said no, because this document was for Defence purposes only.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about this other waiver? At that interview, did the OTP not tell you that they, too, had put in a request for you to be granted a waiver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not put in a request, but official channels were employed through my own institution, there was an official request to Serbia's government which was eventually approved. On the 21st of September, the document was signed and -- hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that, sir. I just ask you my question and you just answer it. There is just one question I have about that. At that interview, were you shown a document in Serbian or a document in English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document that I was shown was in Serbian. And I immediately realised that this had nothing to do with the communication of office business.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just correct something. I think I may have misheard you myself, something you said on page 35, line 7. When you talked about Hadzic's years of military academy, can you please repeat that? Because I think I may have misheard you. I think you said two years, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, Lieutenant Hadzic completed the military academy, and the course was a four-year course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. Sir, you'll be pleased to know that's the end of your questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and your assistance, and you're now free to go back to your ordinary activities. The court officer will show you out. We need to deal with the security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you be so kind as to tell us, briefly, your name first, when and where were you born, and tell us about your family background.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Zirojevic. I was born on the 14th of October, 1963, in Backa Palanka. I'm married and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind -- I would need to ask you a lot of little questions just to bring you through this, but please tell us briefly about your educational background; if and when you completed the military academy; and when you took up your position as a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: In Backa Palanka, my place of birth, I finished elementary and secondary school. Between 1982 and 1986, I attended the military academy, infantry. I was promoted to the rank of second lieutenant on the 26th of July, 1986. After that, I was assigned the duty of a platoon commander in the Brcko garrison. From May 1988, I was officially transferred to the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, slowly, please, for the benefit of the interpreters, list your various duties in the Guards Motorised Brigade before your departure for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in the Guards Motorised Brigade, I was first platoon commander; it was an artillery platoon, a rifle platoon. And then I was the commander of the 2nd Motorised Company in the 1st Motorised Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us about the make-up - and I mean, first and foremost, the ethnic make-up - of the Guards Motorised Brigade before its departure for Vukovar. Can you tell us about that. Can you also tell us about the ethnic make-up of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and I assume the same thing applied to other JNA units, was multi-ethnic, which means there were soldiers with all sorts of different ethnic backgrounds. By the same token, the ethnic make-up of the 1st Motorised Battalion was also multi-ethnic. And here I mean both the officers and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about your company. What was its ethnic make-up? And was it the same back in Belgrade and upon your arrival in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the regular make-up of my company, they came from all sorts of different ethnicities. The commander of one particular platoon was an ethnic Macedonian, the commander of a different platoon was a Serb, and the commander of a third platoon declared himself as an ethnic Yugoslav. The company officer was a Bosnian, a Muslim, and he went to Vukovar with me. As for foot soldiers, there were all the different ethnicities, with the exception of Albanians, but I had also Albanians among my reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were supposed to leave for Vukovar, were there any problems about the ethnic make-up? Were there any refusals and were any consequences suffered by anyone refusing to go to the front? What specifically happened, if anything, in your 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: At the battalion level - and I assume the same thing applied to the brigade - a decision was passed to the effect that soldiers, and officers, too, who did not feel sufficiently fit or mentally fit to carry out combat missions - and this was particularly in reference to recruits aged 18 and 19 at the time - they were given an opportunity to say that they were not willing to go and carry out combat missions. So we applied this. There were soldiers who said they wanted to stay back at the barracks, but there were very few soldiers who did that. In my own company, between five and seven soldiers, I would say, who demanded to stay behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they suffer any consequences because they effectively refused to go to the front?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No consequences were suffered. All those who stayed behind at the barracks were assembled in a temporary unit, and their assignment was to secure the barracks and to make sure there was order in the barracks while the unit itself was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now explain to the Chamber and my friends from the OTP how it was that you eventually ended up going to Vukovar back in 1991? Which month specifically? And where did you first arrive when you reached that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: While we were still at the barracks in Belgrade, we received a preliminary order and we knew what the assignment was facing our unit, the 1st Motorised Battalion, and by that same token, the 2nd Motorised Company, of which I was in command. We received an assignment to carry out the necessary preparations and to conduct a march down the following axis: Belgrade-Sid-Tovarnik. We were also tasked with bringing the unit to a staging area at the Dubrava farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you reached the Dubrava farm, had you been subjected to any attacks from anywhere? Did you come under fire at any time? And how did you reach that area? Can you tell us, in very general terms, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The march began between the 30th of September and the 1st of October. We passed Tovarnik, and up until that point, we had not been attacked. As we were approaching the village of Negoslavci, we came under sporadic sniper fire from the village of Nijemci. We conducted this march in vehicles, which disgorged our troops at the -- upon entering the village of Negoslavci, and we continued our march on foot. We walked from Negoslavci to Vukovar, down the road connecting these two. Two kilometres after Negoslavci there was a road that forked off to Dubrava. As we headed down that road to the farm known as Dubrava, we came under mortar fire. The calibre, I suppose, was 82-millimetre and 62-millimetre mortars, the mortars being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vukovar, were you given a mission, or did you know what the mission would be upon arriving in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As I've pointed out already, back in Belgrade, our battalion commander had given us our previous assignment, which was to conduct a march along the specified axis. It was to take our unit to the staging area there and to be at the ready to attack Vukovar. The objective of that combat mission was to lift the blockade of the barracks there as well as to liberate the population of Vukovar, who had been under siege and under fire and kept that way for some time by Croat paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please say, by way of introduction, what commander's reconnaissance means? How is that term used?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
