utterances.text: Commander's reconnaissance is something that a commander does from the battalion level up, the objective being, before setting out on a combat mission, to specify to his subordinate officers what the specific assignments would be, to each of his subordinate officers, along a given axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Commander's reconnaissance, what exactly does that mean as opposed to komandant reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not essentially. One is from battalion level up and the other is from battalion level down. And it involves a commander's subordinate officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Before you reached the area that you have now described, did your own battalion commander carry out such commander's reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The battalion commander, or rather, the brigade command did, and this involved battalion commanders, so that their assignments would be clear upon their arrival in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that, in keeping with this rule, Major Tesic welcomed you in your area of assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Commander's reconnaissance had been carried out several days before we even set out for Vukovar. The battalion commander and his command was part of the march, part of the battalion's march, and reached the staging area together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try to hurry things along a little since there are a great many facts that we are familiar with based on the evidence of a number of different witnesses. As for the Dubrava farm area, after that you moved on Vukovar. Specifically, you started approaching the Petrova Gora neighbourhood; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you have any scouts who were showing you the way? Or can you tell us more about how you reached that axis. Any guides? Since this was your first time in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The night before we set out for Vukovar, the battalion commander had issued an order to attack. On that occasion, he gave each company two guides who, I suppose, were locals, natives of the Petrova Gora neighbourhood. This means they took us there, when we eventually set out, and took us as far as the confrontation line, which were also our attack positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Assault Detachment 1 means, JOD 1? If so, how exactly was JOD 1, Assault Detachment 1, established in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Assault Detachment 1, at the outset, consisted of the 1st Motorised Battalion and a tank platoon - those were T-84 tanks - as well as a platoon of 20 anti-aircraft guns, 20/3-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What happened later, at stage 2? Since you say, at the outset, it was like this, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: In late October, the JOD was re-established, JOD 1, I'm saying, and again it was made up of the 1st Motorised Battalion, the Petrova Gora TO Detachment, the Leva Supoderica TO Detachment, and a detachment made up of volunteers who had arrived from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who was the commander of JOD 1 at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning, it was Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell us exactly what the axis was of your 2nd Company when you reached the Petrova Gora neighbourhood. Which axis did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The axis of the 2nd Motorised Company was as follows: Svetozara Markovica Street, the 2nd Congress School, and the Bosko Buha neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any volunteer units along your own axis, along the axis of the 2nd Motorised Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the early days of combat, but afterwards there were elements from the Novi Sad volunteer unit involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell us what an observation post is, and can you tell us if you, as a company commander, actually had an observation post.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: An observation post is, for all practical intents, is the place where a platoon commander, a company commander, stays. It is from there that a company commander or a platoon commander exercises command and control over a combat operation, depending on what it is. What we refer to as an observation post is not a stationary thing. It's never in one place only. This very much depends on the nature of combat operations. It can be static or stationary when one is defending, but it has to move when one is attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: For a company commander, was there any observation post along your own axis? Did you have an observation post at the same place where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As I explained, an observation post is where a company commander is staying. If he's staying in a house or on top of a hill, then that's the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the street where you were staying which was the place which was considered the observation post of the command of the 2nd Motorised Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: It was Svetozara Markovica Street, and the building was a catering facility locally known as the Zeplin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us along which axis the 3rd Motorised Company was deployed, the company under the command of Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: If I might digress for a while, I don't have the transcript which you said I would be following on my monitor. Maybe I'm going too fast and maybe I'm making life difficult for the interpreters, but I can hardly know since I don't have the transcript to follow in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the transcript brought up, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I only had your image on my screen a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we're better off that way, for all I know. But, okay, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Motorised Company was the left-hand neighbour of my own company. Its own axis of attack was Petrova Gora, more specifically Nova Street, the neighbourhood known as the 6th Proletarian Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this are of operations in the direction of Milovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: This whole area, the 6th Proletarian Division neighbourhood, the 2nd Congress School, and the Bosko Buha neighbourhood belongs to Milovo Brdo, which is an elevation above the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know where Captain Radic's observation post was, or the place where he slept? Do you know about this; and if so, did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His observation post was at Nova Street - I don't know the house number - but I was there on several occasions, in that house where Captain Radic had his observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you were there, did you ever see or learn or hear that, across the way from there or anywhere nearby, there was some sort of a prison or a detention facility for holding prisoners? Did you ever catch any reference to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was a procedure in place. We knew what we were expected to do with any prisoners. Every time before setting out on a combat mission, each soldier and officer would be given a brochure containing the provisions of the international law of war, and all of us acted in compliance with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say you sometimes went to see Captain Radic at his observation post, the place where he was staying. Did you ever see or hear of any regular meetings taking place there involving members of the Petrova Gora TO and the Leva Supoderica TO detachments, Radic and those two TO detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing I know indicates that. I never saw or heard anything about this taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about the fact that the observation post at Nova Street was being used as a command post for planning operations in order to liberate Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, a company commander cannot set up a command post; he can only establish an observation post. Therefore, this could never have been a command post to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of this military conclusion and your position as a witness, did you ever hear of a staff or a headquarters being there at Nova Street, where the liberation of Vukovar was being planned with Tesic, Sljivancanin, Radic, Vujanovic, and Miroljub Vujovic in attendance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Most definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you now please be so kind as to tell us who Stanko Vujanovic was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he also deployed along the axis of operations of Sasa Bojkovski's company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, he was, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a neighbour of the 3rd Company, as you said, and of Captain Radic, too, did you ever see him along the axis of operations of the 3rd Company, the company under Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zirojevic, would you now please tell us where the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Their command post was also at Svetozara Markovica Street. I can't remember the number, but it was halfway between the rail track and the street leading to Nova Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were regular briefings held at that command post by the company commanders, as they were the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the first few days, that is to say, two or three days, on all other days until the end of combat operations, we had regular briefings at the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who attended these regular briefings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander attended these briefings; then his deputy, Captain Stijakovic, that is; then the company commanders of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, respectively; the commanders of the 120-millimetre Mortar Battery and the armoured company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the mortar company? What was the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Damir Vuckovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber this command post in a bit of detail. What did it mean from a physical point of view? Could anyone come there unannounced? And also, was there anyone who provided security for this command post?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The command battalion has its command post. It is a post where planning takes place, planning of combat activities, that is, and inter alia that is how orders are transmitted to subordinates. That is where the communications equipment is. Security is provided by the military police. No one uninvited can come to the command post, or rather, without the approval of the battalion commander, that is to say, that not just anyone who wishes to can walk in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many buildings are there? Do you remember, after all these years? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the building where the command post was is a single-storey building, and there was an auxiliary building in the yard, a smaller one, one that was smaller from the building where the command post of the battalion command or battalion commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If somebody wanted to listen in to hear what was being said at the briefing, could they actually do that from the auxiliary building? Could they hear the orders and the briefing itself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that was possible. I'm sure it was not possible, in actual fact, because that building is at least about 10 metres away from the main building, if I can call it that, where the regular briefings took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of the name of Dusan Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: It sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he was at the time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: He was introduced to us as the commander of the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard a certain Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was he commander of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at first he led one of these TO groups, Petrova Gora; and later, I think he was appointed commander instead of the mentioned Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in your view, in terms of what your understanding was at the time, who was in command of the Territorial Defence of Petrova Gora and the Leva Supoderica Detachment, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: At first, Jaksic; and after that, Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you had briefings at the command post, did it ever happen that the commanders of TO Petrova Gora and the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment would attend the briefings at the same time when you did?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: In the briefings room, never. For a while, with us, the company commanders, there were none of these other people who were present, Jaksic or Lancuzanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any time when you came to these briefings and when you were receiving orders, did you see at the command post, before or after you were leaving briefings, did you ever see them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times. Either they were leaving as we were coming in, or after our regular briefings, they would be there waiting to be received by the commander of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "to be received," does that mean that they were coming to get their own assignments, irrespective of you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was concerned my learned friend was started to lead down that road. The answer has now been given, but perhaps, in the future, he could be less leading in his questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness gave an answer and it's not in the transcript. "I assume I was not there." It's not in the transcript. After all, I can ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You saw them sometimes before the briefings; sometimes after. What is it that you assumed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I assumed that they came to receive assignments from the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this pleases my learned friend, I would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the companies of the 1st Motorised Battalion, did you have messengers; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Messenger communication is a particular type of communication. At first, going by the rules, we had messengers and we used them up until approximately -- well, it's not approximately. I know the exact date, the 10th of October. Since at that time, in my company, we had a casualty. Ramic Indir, my messenger, a Bosniak, got killed, and also Captain Radic's messenger got killed. And that is when the battalion command made the following decision, since the communications equipment we used until then became unreliable and they could easily be intercepted by the Croatian paramilitary formations, it was decided that messengers would no longer be used but, rather, hand-held radio transmitters, popularly known as Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of your messenger who got killed on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said, a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how this communication took place through these Motorolas that now became an establishment-based system of communication?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: All the officers who had Motorolas were on a single channel, that is to say, that practically we could hear all the conversations that were taking place between any two of the participants involved. It's only that we could not have multiple participation. There could only be two participants in a particular communication, but we could hear everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand properly that all the Motorolas were part of a single network of communications? Or would you call it something different or would you explain it in a different way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Since this type of radio device has several channels, we all used one single channel. We were all on the same channel and we could all hear everyone's conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if the battalion commander is issuing an order to you, as the commander of the 2nd Company, that at the same time this communication between you and the commander of the battalion can be heard by the commanders of the 1st and 3rd Companies, respectively?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, that you said that after the 10th of October, when you introduced Motorolas, you no longer had the need for messenger services?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, so that we could have less movement by soldiers, especially unnecessary movement, because the Croat forces were opening sniper fire. We wanted to reduce movement of soldiers, and that is why we practically did away with the messenger service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to the command post, did you personally, as a company commander, take your own messenger or did you take your own security detail, or did you go on your own?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: At first, yes, until the lines were fortified, but not after that, especially not after the 10th of October. I went alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the case with other company commanders and the commander of the mortar battery?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the order of the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that after the 10th of October, even in that small house that was near the command post, there was no need for any messengers or any soldiers to come there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zirojevic, do you know when Milovo Brdo fell or was liberated, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what your own tasks were then and what the task of Captain Miroslav Radic's company was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Since the command of the battalion concluded that the most favourable way of completing this mission, that is to say, taking Milovo Brdo, was through the 3rd Company, the 3rd Company practically did this; whereas the 1st and 2nd Company cooperated by securing the flanks and the lines attained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Captain Radic's company completed its mission and reached Milovo Brdo, was its further mission to safeguard the taken lines? I don't want to lead --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, my friend is leading on this point. He should ask: After Milovo Brdo, what did the company do next? Not suggest what the task was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're on alert, Mr. Borovic, about the leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Company of Captain Miroslav Radic, to the best of your knowledge, when it reached Milovo Brdo, did it have a mission?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Not only Captain Radic's company, but also the 2nd and the 1st Companies and the mortar battery, once Milovo Brdo was taken, remained at the lines attained and did not have any mission to continue the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "remained at the lines attained," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the area of Milovo Brdo that had been taken was fortified, security was put in place, and we were not engaged in any kind of further movement, since the primary task of the 1st Motorised Battalion, the one that we had received at the outset, at the beginning of the attack, was to take Milovo Brdo, the area of Milovo Brdo. By virtue of that fact, we established control over part of Vukovar that we could not see until then, because the area of Milovo Brdo was not within our vision. We had control over the bridges across the Vuka, linking the old and new part of Vukovar, so to speak. So we had completed our mission, and did not move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "control of the bridges," was that visual, fire, or what type of control? How would you explain it to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it was both visual and fire control of the bridges. From these positions, we could control, by way of fire, any movement of the Croat paramilitary forces. And there was no need to go to the foot of the hill. Tactically, that would have been illogical, because we had positions that were high up and higher up than those of the Croat paramilitary forces. So it was virtually impossible because it is a very steep slope below Milovo Brdo, so you couldn't really go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you remain in the area of Milovo Brdo? And after that mission to fortify the taken area, when was your next task and when did you get it? I'm referring to the companies of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: After Milovo Brdo was taken, and at the proposal of the deputy battalion commander, we asked, or rather, the battalion command asked, that the 1st Motorised Battalion, since it had carried out its mission, should remain at the lines attained and that the other parts of the brigade should carry out their assignment. This was accepted by the brigade command, and I think that on the 14th this was definitely regulated, that is to say that the 1st Motorised Battalion got out of the assault detachment and remained in the area of Milovo Brdo, ready to engage along some other axis and support other units from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point in time from the 10th until the fall of Vukovar, in the area of Milovo Brdo, did the members of TO Petrova Gora and the Leva Supoderica Detachment ever take part in securing the lines attained with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the decision reached on the 14th and earlier on, that is to say, from the 10th onwards practically, they were no longer within the composition, or rather, these positions. And according to the decision of the brigade, or rather, the Operations Group South of the 14th of November, the 1st Assault Detachment consisted of those units without the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Not to go into interpreting various orders and decisions; I did that several times here and I do not want to tire the Trial Chamber with that. I am now asking you about the factual situation. On the 10th of November and up to the fall of Vukovar, the members of TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica, did they, together with you, take part in securing the attained lines?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: From the fall of Milovo Brdo, Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica no longer acted in concert with the 1st Battalion in carrying out its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was Vukovar liberated? And how did you find out about the liberation of Vukovar? Did someone tell you? Who told you? In what way did you find out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As for information about that, that the handover of Vukovar, or rather, that the Croat paramilitary forces were surrendering, I heard about that in the early morning hours of the 18th of November. Specifically, I was on the rim of Milovo Brdo, in a part of Milovo Brdo that the local population calls Drvena Pijaca, the log market or timber market, Captain Radic and Captain Bojkovski were there, too, and Lieutenant Hadzic told us this. He was a platoon commander in Captain Radic's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, 1991, did you - and I mean your three companies - move, or rather, were you still in the Milovo Brdo area on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because Milovo Brdo is not just the elevation itself but also the surrounding area, including the timber market that I mentioned. That is also part of Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think there's an interpretation problem, so can you please describe this place you refer to as the timber market. What does that mean, the timber market?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was in that area that timber was bought and sold. It's a small square with a petrol station right in the middle of it. The square was a confluence of five or six different streets from different parts of town. It's a rather small square, and one of its typical features was the presence of a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that on the 19th you happened to be in the timber market, which was part of the Milovo Brdo area. My question: You personally, as the commander of the 2nd Company of the 1st Motorised Battalion, were you given any specific tasks by your commander, since you say that Vukovar fell on that day, the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. I was told to take my soldiers and cross a bridge over at Vuka River, head straight for the Danube Hotel, which was at the point where the Vuka River flows into the Danube. I was told to search that building since we had received information to indicate that a man known as Jastreb, who was the commander of Croat paramilitary formations, had previously established his headquarters there and was still hiding in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, on that day, or rather, at that time, Captain Miroslav Radic was also given an assignment? Just briefly, because we're about to have a break. Do you know that? And what was the assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I received my assignment over a Motorola from the battalion commander, Major Tesic. After that, he handed out an assignment to Captain Radic, too, since we were all part of a single network. He told him to take his soldiers, go to the hospital area, set up a security regime outside the hospital, and allow no one in or out until we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's not an objection on this occasion, but more asking for clarification. My learned friend asked the question on page 62, at line 7, in respect of the 19th, and Mr. Zirojevic being in the timber market. Further on in the paragraph he says: "Since you say that Vukovar fell that day, the 18th of November." There seems to be some confusion, perhaps due to translation, but certainly with the transcript I have, there seems to be different dates talked about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to follow that up at all, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on what day Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you at the timber market on the 19th of November, at the foot of Milovo Brdo, when you received that first assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you heard whether other company commanders and the commander of the mortar battery received their assignments much the same way as you did, over a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the commander of the mortar battery was told to be at the ready, since the situation was still not clear-cut, and that other attacks were still expected by minor groups who had refused to surrender. They were told to be at the ready in order to open fire in the eventuality of an attack by one of those minor groups. Further, Captain Bojkovski was ordered to stay with his unit in that same area, at the ready, in order to step in should there be any further acts of provocation by those minor units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a convenient time for the break? I think I've slightly lost my bearings, so I'm not sure. If so, I move that we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the right time for the break, and we will resume at 6.00 because of a redaction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you got this assignment on the 19th of November, did you go and carry it out? And did you carry it out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Having received the assignment, I sent one soldier, one officer, on foot, and I drove there in a vehicle. I searched the hotel building from the basement to the upper most floor. In the meantime I had been given the assignment of preparing the conference room of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. I see an error in the transcript. I will repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I sent the commander of my platoon, from my company that means, with soldiers to go there. They walked and I drove after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's all right, because the transcript says "I sent one soldier."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I received a new assignment. The assignment was to prepare a conference room and clear it, because there was all sorts of rubble in that room, since there was to be a press conference in that conference room on the following day. Having searched the hotel, I continued with this other mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, the only people on that mission were soldiers and officers from your company, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the Leva Supoderica TO Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the evening of the 19th, did you have a regular briefing? And who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As any other day, there was a briefing on the evening of the 19th. The battalion commander was there, Major Tesic; his deputy, Captain Stijakovic; the company commanders; and the commander of the 120-millimetre mortar battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following day, the 20th of November, were you still on this mission at the Danube Hotel; if so, for how long? What exactly went on? Can you tell us anything that we might find of interest here in this courtroom? What happened by the regular briefing on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I left behind at the Danube Hotel as security an officer from my unit, with about ten other soldiers, to secure the hotel building. The next morning, with the remainder of the soldiers whom I had pulled back to our area of deployment previously, I went back to the Danube Hotel and continued with the preparations for this press conference, clearing and cleaning the conference room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, did you have the impression or was there anything for you to indicate who had been in the Danube Hotel during combat operations prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: There had been indications that a man named Jastreb, who was in the command of the Croat paramilitary forces, had been staying there. We even found a vehicle when we arrived, one that had been destroyed. It was not in good working order. And there was also some equipment, some communication devices, some documents. I didn't really look closely what the documents were. That was one of the reasons for the hotel to be thoroughly searched, because there was a certain likelihood that some remaining members of the Croat paramilitary formations were still there. This is a tall building; therefore, there was also the likelihood of snipers still present in the building. And that was another reason why we conducted this search.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So the following day you continued this mission, you carried on with this mission. Did anyone from your superior command come to see you? Did anyone from the other companies belonging to the 1st Motorised Battalion come to see you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That morning, Captain Radic came several times. At about noon, possibly early afternoon, Captain Stijakovic arrived as well to check how far we had got with our preparations, and he stayed a while with Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that on the 20th of November, the second day of your missions, Stijakovic arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I know because we sat there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it not, perhaps, Borivoje Tesic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I know because we sat together, and I gave Captain Stijakovic an interesting bottled drink as a gift. It was on some sort of a metal swing, and it was half vermouth -- on a seesaw. It was half vermouth and half something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you have your regular briefing on the evening of the 20th? Who was there? And did you see any TO members or people from the Leva Supoderica Detachment anywhere near?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As any other day, we held a regular briefing that evening, which meant that reports were submitted on any missions carried out over the course of the day. And another thing that was done is that missions were handed out for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which specific assignments did you receive on the evening of the 19th and which on the evening of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th, I was told to carry on with the preparations for that press conference. Having completed that, I was to carry on gathering any equipment left behind during combat operations. On the evening of the 20th --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: For a short while, 20 minutes, half an hour, the battalion commander was there, and then he left and said he was on his way to the brigade command. And the deputy commander, Captain Stijakovic, was also there; the company commanders and the commander of the mortar battery. As for the assignment I got on the evening of the 20th --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Hold it right there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe there might be an error in the transcript at page 67. Let me just take a minute to find that. Mr. Borovic's question was: "Were members of the TO and Leva Supoderica ..." and it says: "Members of the TO from Leva Supoderica," which would imply that this was one and the same thing. So if Mr. Borovic could please rephrase that question because I think both the question and the answer have been erroneously recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend for giving me a hand with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So, did any of the Petrova Gora TO Detachment or the Leva Supoderica TO Detachment assist you with carrying out this mission at the Danube Hotel on the 19th or 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Most certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the evening of the 20th, was Radic wearing the same sort of uniform that all of you company commanders in the 1st Motorised Battalion had been wearing up to that point? Or did you, perhaps, spot a difference?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not only 20th. It was on the 19th that he stopped wearing the same uniform that we had been wearing up to that point. He got a camouflage uniform, which we had not been familiar with up to that point in time. It was only later to be introduced as part of standard-issue JNA equipment, a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 20th of November, at the briefing that evening, Radic was wearing this camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 20th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 20th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, when he came to the Danube Hotel, was he wearing that same uniform that he had -- just a minute, please -- that he had worn at the 19th of November briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You say that after a while Major Tesic was off somewhere. Do you know where it was that he went to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that he was on his way to the brigade command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is an overlap between different voices and we find it impossible to follow the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you're asked to slow and to leave a space between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will comply with this caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, please, when you hear my question, wait and then answer slowly. Thank you. Who took over command of the 1st Motorised Battalion after Tesic left on the 20th of November, 1991? And how long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: It was his deputy, Captain Stijakovic, that took over, and this went on until the return of Major Tesic from Belgrade, which was on the following day, the afternoon or possibly the evening of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he give you any orders in relation to the following day, Captain Stijakovic, in his capacity as the deputy of the battalion commander? And what sort of assignment did you receive, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to those known to us from earlier on, we were also given the following assignment: The following day, the 21st, in the morning, Captain Stijakovic said he would be reviewing troops, soldiers, and officers alike in each of the units, in their own areas of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he more specific? Which units was he supposed to review? Can you please wait for the interpretation to finish. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: He said -- or he ordered, or rather, he told us to prepare for this and said that he would be reviewing the companies, each of the companies, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he order a review of the mortar battery as well, or did that go without out saying when he said "companies," because, from the point of view of establishment, it was a company. And what about the commander, Damir Vuckovic [as interpreted], did he attend the briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The mortar battery is considered to be a company. It is at company level, so that is why I am not mentioning it specifically in every answer. And Mr. Vuckovic was present at this briefing. The review also involved his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, two times we have the name "Damir" in the transcript but it's supposed to be "Davor," Davor Vuckovic. This must be a mistake in the interpretation, so we don't want problems later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the commander of the mortar battery?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Davor Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it right. Where did you go after the briefing on the 20th of November, 1991, you, personally? And where did the others go from this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of this briefing, the commander of the mortar battery, Vuckovic, invited all of those present to be his guests that evening at the house that he used for rest, because he had prepared dinner there, a modest dinner. His soldiers got a pig from the locals, so he invited all of us who had been present there. After this regular briefing, I went to the deployment area of my own unit. I ordered activities with a view to preparing the review that was supposed to take place on the following day. And then after that I went to that house that the commander of the mortar battery had been using for his own rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who else came to this dinner from the command post? Was Stijakovic present? Did he come to this dinner?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my friend is entitled to ask who was at this dinner; he's not entitled to tell the witness the names in advance. Again, he's leading the witness in a very important aspect of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you'd take notice, thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After the briefing, who came, if anybody did, to this dinner at Davor Vuckovic's?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: From the battalion command, Sergeant Bojic came, Staff Sergeant Bojic. Captain Stijakovic expressed his thanks for the invitation, but since the commander of the battalion was not at his command post, he quite simply could not leave the command post. He could not leave it, since there were no other officers there who could be in charge of the command post. Then Captain Radic was present. I think he first went to the area of deployment of his company and then he came to this house that Vuckovic had been using for rest. That is as far as those who were present at the briefing were concerned. The commander of the 1st Company wasn't there and of the armoured company either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did you stay? And can you give us a more graphic description of what it was that you did there. Briefly, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was an opportunity to relax after a long time without thinking about possible attacks and combat activities, so that is what we did, roughly. We relaxed. We drank, ate, sang. So it was a relaxed atmosphere, practically as if we were not in the situation that we were in. So we were sort of decompressing after all the stress that we had gone through over the preceding two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And until when, approximately, did you stay at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the exact hour was, but I know that it was just before dawn. Actually, it had already started dawning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we already heard several times in this courtroom persons referring to food and drink during the Vukovar operation. My question was: Were you hungry during these operations, or thirsty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: We were not hungry or thirsty, but if I tell you that during those 50-something days I had a cooked meal only twice and the rest of the time I was eating only canned food, you can assume how enjoyable that was for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that, perhaps, the reason why you remember this dinner so well, the first time after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: My friend is giving the witness an answer in advance as to why he remembers this dinner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, Mr. Lunny has made very clear that he would object to leading on these matters, and you are quite often now leading on matters of some significance in this case. If you would take care. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that my learned friend Mr. Lunny likes to imitate me a bit. I like this way of communicating professionally; he's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, in addition to this relaxation, what it was like. Who sat where; do you remember? If you can, try; if not, just tell us you cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: I am waiting for the transcript to finish so that I start my answer. So, in addition to the persons I mentioned, there were a few soldiers there, Captain Vuckovic's soldiers; then the owner of that house that was being used by Captain Vuckovic for rest; then there were a few of his neighbours there. I know that the owner of the house sat at this long table. I know that he sat at the head of the table on one side, and that at the other side, at the head of the table, there was Vuckovic, whereas Radic and I sat opposite each other, next to Vuckovic. As for the rest, the other soldiers and civilians, or rather, neighbours, they were there on the sides, on some benches. On one side there were benches, and on the other side there were chairs. And I also think that there was this dining arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that it was almost morning when you parted, did you carry out your task? Or did the review take place where your company was; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Since, after the briefing, I issued a task to the platoon commander from my company to prepare this, the review had been prepared by morning. Specifically, the review of my company was at 9.00 in the morning. Of course, when I arrived I went to sleep and -- but I did get up, observing the orders of the deputy commander, and I was present at the review.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During combat operations in Vukovar, were any of your soldiers wounded or killed? I'm referring to soldiers from your company.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I had wounded soldiers and I had killed soldiers, both soldiers and officers. Perhaps I could illustrate this by saying that I took 120 soldiers to Vukovar and returned 20 from Vukovar. I believe that that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you return from Vukovar to Belgrade, on what date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of November, in the morning hours, that's when we left, and we arrived in barracks, in Belgrade, around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for this task that you had at the Danube Hotel and then on the 21st the task that had to do with the review, what about the remaining two days before you went to Belgrade? Did you have any special assignments or -- or what were you doing? What tasks did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: The task was along the axis of attack, every company along the axis of its own attack should collect equipment, arms, ammunition, explosives, mines; to have all the combat kits right; to have the soldiers in proper condition, that they should all get haircuts, and so on; practically cleaning up the terrain in terms of military equipment, gathering this military equipment; and preparing for return to Belgrade; and perhaps carrying out another task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the Vukovar operation, on the axis where you were, as well as the 3rd Company, up to Milovo Brdo, the liberation of Milovo Brdo, was there artillery fire at your positions by the paramilitary formations? And what do you know about that? I'm referring to Croat paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course we were under artillery fire. I've already explained that this happened when we came to the area of deployment at Dubrava farm. That was the first time. And the next time was when we set out to carry out our assignment, attack. There was terrible mortar fire and other artillery fire in the Petrova Gora neighbourhood. Of course, during combat activity, practically every day we were under mortar fire and fire coming from other artillery pieces. The death of soldier Ramic that I already referred to, I mean he was seriously wounded by a mortar shell. After that, he bled to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zirojevic, can you tell the Trial Chamber who Captain Miroslav Radic is during the Vukovar operation, before, and after the Vukovar operations. During this time as a commander, komandir, how did he behave? And how could you describe him as a human being and as a professional? What is it that you know about him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Radic is a very honourable, honest, and professional officer. At the time when he was a professional military man, if he had not been that kind of person, I believe that he could not have been a member of the Guards Brigade, as the most elite unit of the Yugoslav People's Army. He's a family man, the father of two children; highly responsible towards his family and his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically, since you were neighbours, what were the comments made with regard to his courage, discipline, his self- initiative? Can you tell us a bit more about that, because this would be the end of the examination-in-chief, and you are a witness who can give us a closer description of what can be said about him personally and from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Radic could not take any initiative of his own because there was no such thing in the Guards Brigade. There was no self-initiative. So he behaved in accordance with the tasks that he received from the battalion command, or rather, the battalion commander. So, during combat activities, he could not do anything on his own; should not have done anything on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the discipline that prevailed in his 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: During these combat activities, we were often in contact. I'm not only taking into account the regular briefings, but during the actual combat actions, practically every day, since we were neighbours and since we had to fortify our positions. After the end, when night fell, it was impossible to carry out any kind of combat activity, and no movement was allowed. I know that once he told me that he had problems with a certain group of reserve soldiers and that he sent them back, or rather, sent them away from his unit. They tried to introduce defeatism to make the rest of the troops rebel, so he sent them away so his unit would not fall apart, that it would, rather, carry out its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he strict and did he mete out punishment, or did he behave in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by "punishment."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could he punish people, or did he resolve things in a different way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, punishment was actually disciplinary action. No torture, no physical mistreatment, beatings, tying up of soldiers; soldiers or officers could not be punished in that way. Only disciplinary measures were taken for any infraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear from anyone that Captain Radic was responsible for what happened at Ovcara, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Most certainly not. And knowing him as a person, I would find that inconceivable. He, quite simply, could not do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed the examination-in-chief of this witness, and now he is here, ready to answer other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Domazet, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zirojevic, I am Vladimir Domazet, attorney-at-law, Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic. I just have a few questions for you, quite simply to some things that I, perhaps, did not understand. So I'm going to ask you, perhaps, even to repeat some answers so that I will not lead you, although this is cross-examination. You will remember - and now I'm asking you once again - who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: At first, as far as I know, it was a certain Jaksic, Captain Jaksic, and after that, again, as far as I know, Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And the commander of Leva Supoderica, you've already spoken about that, too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: A man named Lancuzanin, Milan Lancuzanin, unless I'm wrong, nicknamed Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Something else about that. Did he remain as a commander until the very end, or was he, at one point, removed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he remained throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another thing you said about Major Tesic, I think, on the 20th. You were asked and you provided an answer, but because of the speed, your answer was not recorded in its entirety, so that there still remains something that is not quite clear because there was an intervention by the interpreter saying that there was overlap between the different voices and microphones. Now, my clarification is: Where did Major Tesic go on the evening of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: He stayed at the briefing briefly and then he said he was off to Negoslavci, to the brigade command post or the operations group command post. He said that after he'd be off to Belgrade, because the following day there was a reception for Motorised Guards Brigade officers at the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the following day, the 21st, he was no longer in Negoslavci; he was away. I think you said that when you talked about the review.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Lukic -- I'm sorry. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am one of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence counsel. I have merely a handful of questions, issues of interest to the Sljivancanin Defence team. It's about the following: During your time in Vukovar, your assignments and any combat missions that you describe, were you in touch with Veselin Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these contacts between you? And where did these contacts occur?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: As the chief of security of the brigade, he would tour all the units along the front line, and that was where we met, depending on where my observation post was at a given point in time. He wanted to know about the situation prevailing in our unit in terms of morale, in terms of security. He wanted to know about the activities taken by the enemy --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. He wanted to know about the activities undertaken by the Croatian paramilitary units. He wanted to know about the situation that prevailed in my company in the sense of there being any soldiers trying to stoke up a rebellion of some sort. Most of all, he wanted to know about anything that might have adversely affected the security situation in the unit and thereby the unit's mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During these contacts between you and Veselin Sljivancanin, did he ever try to issue you an order, or did he effectively order anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the sense of carrying out a mission. Never. In principle, he would not have had the power to issue me an order without my superior command being informed, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At these regular briefings at the battalion commanders, the briefings that you spoke about in reply to my learned friend Mr. Borovic's questions, did you ever hear from anyone present at the briefing about people saying that Major Sljivancanin had issued anyone any order at all, since he was, after all, as you said yourself, touring all the units along the front line?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything of that nature. And besides, it is the duty of an officer, having received an order from a superior command level, to inform his direct superior accordingly. More specifically, if, for example, a brigade commander issues an order to a company commander, this company commander is duty-bound to, first of all, carry out this order and to inform the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this now. You answered questions by Mr. Borovic about the ethnic make-up of the Guards Brigade and the ethnic make-up of your own unit. What I want to know is: Did all the members of your company, regardless of their ethnicity, take part in combat action that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you brought 120 men to Vukovar and came back with a mere 20, which would mean that 100 people were put out of action at some point, at various points during the campaign. Among those killed, were there any Croats or people belonging to other ethnicities - Albanians, Bosnians, Slovaks, Hungarians, what have you - if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there were. The first soldier ever to be wounded, a member of my company, was an ethnic Croat, Goran Dencic, who was a sharpshooter in his own squad. I already mentioned the late Indir Ramic, who was a Bosniak. There was another Croat soldier who was wounded; he was -- then there was the commander of the 3rd Platoon, Marijan Catelevski [phoen], who was an ethnicity Macedonian. As far as loss, retrievable losses, so to speak, those who were put out of action as a result of high stress and were consequently sent back, so not entirely put out of action you might say, there were situations, such as the one in late October, where our reservists were sent back -- our reserve soldiers and officers returned to Belgrade, in actual fact, the reason being the federal government had adopted a decision to the effect that any reservist could only be kept in a unit for as long as 45 days. And that is one of the reasons why you have this 100-men discrepancy. But there certainly were losses as well that were sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Slobodan Popovic, Sergeant Slobodan Popovic, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain who this person is. And do you know what became of him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Sergeant Popovic was in Major Sljivancanin's closest security circle. He died on the 6th of October, 1991. He was killed outside my own observation post. I saw him being killed with my own eyes. If you want me to explain what exactly happened, I'd be glad to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please try. Was there anything unusual about this? And what was the late Sergeant Popovic doing with Major Sljivancanin at your observation post?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: That day I had suffered certain losses on account of the mortar fire of the Croat paramilitary forces. I wasn't able to evacuate the wounded with my own men, so I did whatever I could. I applied some makeshift measures to stop the bleeding, to dress their wounds. And then I applied to the battalion command, since the firing was still going on, to send me a vehicle that I could use to withstand that firing. After about half an hour, 45 minutes, a combat vehicle emerged with a caterpillar. This was an infantry combat vehicle. The vehicle disgorged Major Sljivancanin. Major Sljivancanin walked into the front yard, followed by the late Sergeant Popovic. I saw an enemy bullet hit him with my very own eyes. His body was on the ground, and he was hit about another dozen time by bullets. The driver remained inside the vehicle, and then we asked him, the driver of the combat vehicle, to get into the front yard in order for us to be able to evacuate the wounded from that building. As he was manoeuvreing the vehicle, he simply drove over Sergeant Popovic's body, flattening him there. It was an ugly scene. I'm not sure what to say. A disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was his body evacuated, pulled out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: We used a metal hook attached to a length of rope, the principal purpose of which was to remove booby-traps or anti-tank mines with an additional fuse that was not visible to the naked eye. And using this metal hook attached to a string or a length of rope, you make sure the distance is sufficient. If you pull it out like that, there are no casualties and no one is hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why this method was used in order to evacuate the body of the late Sergeant Popovic? What was the reason for that? Just to avoid being leading.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we simply couldn't reach the body because of the heavy firing that we were subjected to by the Croatian side, their sharpshooters, especially because they were using armour-piercing dumdum bullets that caused a lot of panic. They would make a sound when exploding, and that created even more fear, even more panic among the soldiers and officers. But most of all, because of the sniper fire, this was the only way we could get the body out. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, let me ask you this to wrap things up: Popovic was hit by a sniper; his body was lying on the ground and still being showered and riddled with bullets. There is this combat vehicle, a caterpillar, helping the wounded to get away. What sort of effect did that have on all of you present there, including Major Sljivancanin? How exactly were you affected by this scene that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC
utterances.text: It had a disastrous effect; it had a demoralising effect. We were speechless; we were deeply sorry. I happened to know this man personally and it really affected me in a very bad way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Mr. Zirojevic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Now, Mr. Lunny, it's ten to. Is it practical to start now or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in Your Honour's hands in that regard. I'm certainly happy to start just now, but the first set of questions I have would run for more than ten minutes and I don't think there's any natural break in that set of the evidence, in that section of the evidence. And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, in the circumstances, we will adjourn now and continue tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
